original_interpretation: On 4 March 2025 President Trump said CHIPS Act recipients 'don't spend' their awards and that Congress should get rid of the CHIPS Act.
evidence_found: "On March 4, 2025, President Trump critiqued the CHIPS Act, stating that the companies that received awards under the CHIPS Act 'don't spend' the awards to construct and expand semiconductor fabs." and "You [Congress] should get rid of the CHIP[S] Act. And whatever is left over, Mr. Speaker, you should use it to reduce debt or any other reason you want to." (CRS R49031, 14 Jul 2026, re-opened 2026-09-30)
notes: Researcher's quote was a paraphrase stitched into one sentence; CRS wording differs slightly but substance matches.

original_interpretation: FY2026 is the last year for which the CHIPS Act of 2022 provides advance appropriations to Commerce for semiconductor manufacturing incentives.
evidence_found: "FY2026 is the last year for which the CHIPS Act of 2022 provides future year appropriations to DOC for incentivizing the domestic production of semiconductors as authorized in Section 9902 of the FY2021 NDAA." (CRS R49031, 14 Jul 2026, re-opened 2026-09-30)

original_interpretation: CRS states the 35% semiconductor investment tax credit is available only to projects that begin fab construction before 31 December 2026.
evidence_found: "The 35% investment tax credit for capital expenses associated with the production of semiconductors and equipment for manufacturing semiconductors is available only to projects that begin fab construction before December 31, 2026." (CRS R49031, 14 Jul 2026, re-opened 2026-09-30)
notes: Claim correctly attributes the wording to CRS. The statute (48D(e), quoted in T.D. 10009 preamble) excludes property 'the construction of which begins after December 31, 2026', so construction beginning on 31 Dec 2026 itself still qualifies; CRS's 'before' is marginally imprecise. See CON-0029.

original_interpretation: Expected completion dates of the 40 CHIPS-funded fab projects span November 2024 to October 2033.
evidence_found: "Awardees' expected completion dates span from November 2024 to October 2033." Also: "By January 31, 2025, NIST's CPO had awarded 19 companies with a total of up to $30.7 billion in funding for 40 commercial semiconductor fab projects." (CRS R49031, 14 Jul 2026, re-opened 2026-09-30)

original_interpretation: Intel announced in February 2025 that it would delay the opening of its New Albany, Ohio fab from 2026 to 2030; as of June 2026 CRS reported Intel was continuing construction.
evidence_found: "Intel announced in February 2025 that it would delay the opening of its planned fab in New Albany, OH, from 2026 to 2030" ... "As of June 2026, Intel is continuing to build the fab in New Albany." (CRS R49031, 14 Jul 2026, re-opened 2026-09-30)

original_interpretation: Micron announced in November 2025 that it would delay the expected opening of its first fab in Clay, New York from 2028 to the third quarter of 2030.
evidence_found: "Micron announced in November 2025 that it would delay the anticipated opening of its first planned fab in Clay, NY, from 2028 to the third quarter of 2030." (CRS R49031, 14 Jul 2026, re-opened 2026-09-30)

original_interpretation: TSMC delayed its second Arizona fab by at least a year in January 2024, citing uncertainty over its CHIPS award among other reasons.
evidence_found: "TSMC announced in January 2024—after the NOFO and before receiving its PMT—that the start of production at its second planned fab in Arizona would be delayed by at least a year and cited uncertainties with the CHIPS Act funding award as one of the reasons." (CRS R49031, 14 Jul 2026, re-opened 2026-09-30)

original_interpretation: Amkor moved its planned Peoria, Arizona facility to another site in September 2025 and shifted expected production start from 2027 to 2028.
evidence_found: "Another award recipient, Amkor Technologies, moved the site for its planned facility from one location to another in Peoria, AZ. ... This site change coincided with the company's moving of the anticipated start of production from 2027 to 2028." (CRS R49031, 14 Jul 2026, re-opened 2026-09-30)
correction: The CRS text does not date the site move to September 2025; it only cites a footnoted media source dated 5 September 2025. The site move and the 2027-to-2028 production shift are supported; the 'September 2025' timing is an inference from the footnote date.
notes: CRS also notes the Peoria government attributed the move to 'market demands ... and increased project scope' and a media report cited resident pushback over wastewater.

original_interpretation: In late August 2025 the Commerce Department declared void the agreement granting Natcast up to US$7.4 billion of CHIPS R&D funding to operate the NSTC, and said NIST would assume operation of the NSTC.
evidence_found: Manufacturing Dive (27 Aug 2025): "The Department of Commerce announced on Monday that it's voiding up to $7.4 billion in CHIPS and Science Act funding allocated for the nonprofit National Center for the Advancement of Semiconductor Technology Center known as Natcast." and (paraphrase) operational responsibility for the NSTC transferred to NIST. AIP FYI (26 Nov 2025): Lutnick announced in late August he was "clawing back" $7.4 billion from Natcast.
notes: Two independent trade-press publishers (tier 2); Commerce's own announcement/letter was not opened. $7.4bn is an up-to ceiling, correctly flagged in metric.population.

original_interpretation: Commerce Secretary Lutnick's 25 August 2025 letter to Natcast argued that the previous administration had no specific legal authority to create Natcast, citing the Government Corporation Control Act.
evidence_found: Manufacturing Dive (27 Aug 2025): letter dated 25 August 2025 to Natcast CEO Deirdre Hanford citing the Government Corporation Control Act; quote: "The Department under the Biden Administration had no specific legal authorization to establish Natcast as it did — the CHIPS Act does not contain a provision specifically permitting the creation of a corporation to serve as the operator of the NSTC."
notes: reported_claim is correct classification (Lutnick's legal position, not an established legal finding). Letter itself not opened; verified against trade-press account.

original_interpretation: After taking back the NSTC, the administration cancelled the three planned NSTC facilities: the EUV Accelerator at Albany NanoTech (planned to cost up to US$825 million), the design and collaboration facility in California and the advanced packaging piloting facility in Arizona.
evidence_found: AIP FYI (26 Nov 2025): Commerce would "initially spend up to $825 million to stand up the Extreme Ultraviolet Accelerator facility" (Albany); "a Design and Collaboration Facility in California" and "an Advanced Packaging Piloting Facility in Arizona" listed among the three facilities that will not move forward.

original_interpretation: On 24 September 2025 NIST's CHIPS R&D Office issued Broad Agency Announcement 2025-NIST-CHIPS-CRDO-01 soliciting research, prototyping and commercial-solution proposals, open on a rolling basis through September 2029.
evidence_found: NIST news (24 Sep 2025): BAA "soliciting proposals for research, prototyping and commercial solutions that advance U.S. microelectronics technology"; proposals considered "on a rolling basis". Covington (5 Nov 2025): "Broad Agency Announcement No. 2025-NIST-CHIPS-CRDO-01", active "through September 2029, and awards will be issued on a rolling basis." NIST CRDO BAA page (updated 28 Sep 2026): "may be submitted by or before September 30, 2029, via grants.gov."
correction: Accurate as of issuance, but the BAA has since changed: on 20 April 2026 it was revised into two paths (Investment Fund Path and R&D Project Path), and on 2 September 2026 CRDO announced a temporary pause from 15 September 2026, with applications expected to reopen in November 2026. See the new claim recorded in this batch.
notes: BAA number and Sept 2029 end date confirmed on NIST's own CRDO BAA page (tier 1).

original_interpretation: The 2025 CHIPS R&D broad agency announcement states that applicants may be required to give Commerce equity, warrants, IP licences, royalties, revenue sharing or similar instruments, a departure from earlier CHIPS R&D programmes.
evidence_found: Covington (5 Nov 2025): the Department may require applicants to provide "equity, warrants, licenses to intellectual property, royalties, revenue sharing, or other such instruments", described as "a departure from previously-established CHIPS Act programs." AIP FYI (26 Nov 2025): "awardees may be required to issue royalties or otherwise share revenue with the Commerce Department."
correction: The instrument list and the 'departure' characterisation come only from a law-firm blog (tier 3) quoting the BAA; the BAA PDF itself (nist.gov .../CRDO%20BAA_final.pdf) returned 404 and the NIST news release and CRDO BAA page do not mention equity or warrants. Royalties/revenue sharing are corroborated by AIP (tier 2). 'Departure from earlier programmes' is Covington's characterisation, not BAA text.

original_interpretation: Deputy Commerce Secretary Paul Dabbar described the broad agency announcement as the primary mechanism for CHIPS R&D awards, with a stated aim of moving on a business-like timeline.
evidence_found: AIP FYI (26 Nov 2025): NIST issued the solicitation as "the primary mechanism" for the department to make awards for the NSTC and other CHIPS R&D programs; Dabbar: "this process is intended to be nimble and capable of moving on a business-like timeline."

original_interpretation: TSMC provides an irrevocable, absolute and unconditional parent guarantee to the Commerce Department for TSMC Arizona's financial obligations under its CHIPS direct funding and loan agreements, and the awards are subject to conditions and project-milestone requirements.
evidence_found: "In connection with the Direct Funding Agreement and the Loan Agreements, the Company entered into certain guarantee agreements, under which the Company agrees to provide an irrevocable, absolute and unconditional guarantee to the DOC regarding any financial obligations owed by TSMC Arizona to the DOC. The awards under the Direct Funding Agreement are subject to various conditions, compliance requirements, program requirements and project milestone requirements." (TSMC Form 20-F FY2025, text extracted from PDF 2026-09-30, PDF p. 31, Item 4)

original_interpretation: Under its CHIPS loan guarantee agreement TSMC Arizona is entitled to draw down up to US$5 billion in government loans for its Phoenix projects.
evidence_found: "TSMC Arizona also entered into a loan guarantee agreement and several ancillary agreements with the DOC (the 'Loan Agreements'), under which TSMC Arizona is entitled to draw down up to US$5 billion in government loans for the Projects." (TSMC Form 20-F FY2025, text extracted from PDF 2026-09-30, PDF p. 31, Item 4)
notes: Same passage: direct funding award up to US$6.6 billion (Nov 2024).

original_interpretation: TSMC received NT$76,258.8 million of government grants in 2025 (NT$75,164.3 million in 2024) across subsidiaries TSMC Arizona, ESMC, JASM and TSMC Nanjing, without disclosing the US CHIPS share.
evidence_found: "For the years ended December 31, 2023, 2024 and 2025, TSMC received a total of NT$47,545.9 million, NT$75,164.3 million and NT$76,258.8 million as government grants respectively." (TSMC Form 20-F FY2025, text extracted from PDF 2026-09-30, PDF p. 162, Note 30 Government Grants)
notes: No country split disclosed in Note 30.

original_interpretation: TSMC's FY2025 20-F notes that TSMC Arizona is also eligible to apply for a 25% investment grant for its qualified investments, a description that does not reflect the 35% rate enacted in 2025 for property placed in service after 2025.
evidence_found: "The agreements include the construction timelines and other conditions that must be complied with. TSMC Arizona is also eligible to apply for a 25% investment grant for its qualified investments." (TSMC Form 20-F FY2025, text extracted from PDF 2026-09-30, PDF p. 162, Note 30)
correction: The 20-F statement is verified. The second clause ('does not reflect the 35% rate') is the researcher's interpretation, not a fact from the source; for FY2025 the 25% rate was correct for property placed in service through 31 Dec 2025 (IRS 48D page), so the 20-F is not wrong for the period it covers.
notes: claim_type 'fact' fits only the first clause; the second clause should be an interpretation.

original_interpretation: TSMC's 20-F lists as a risk that CHIPS incentives may not be received at anticipated levels and may carry conditions such as restrictions on expanding facilities in foreign countries of concern and on joint research and technology licensing.
evidence_found: "there is no assurance that we will be able to receive such financial incentives, including pursuant to the U.S. CHIPS Act, at the levels we anticipate or at all. Additionally, any financial incentives we receive may be subject to conditions and requirements imposed by the grantors, such as restrictions on the expansion of facilities in foreign countries of concern and on joint research and technology licensing efforts with foreign entities of concern" (TSMC Form 20-F FY2025, text extracted from PDF 2026-09-30, PDF p. 13, Item 3 Risk Factors)

original_interpretation: Intel's final CHIPS commercial award (up to US$7.86 billion, November 2024) was smaller than its preliminary award because Congress required CHIPS funds to pay for the US$3 billion Secure Enclave programme.
evidence_found: "The final total award is less than the proposed preliminary award due to a congressional requirement to use CHIPS funding to pay for the $3 billion Secure Enclave program." and "awarded Intel up to $7.86 billion in direct funding" (Intel 8-K Ex. 99.1, 26 Nov 2024, re-opened 2026-09-30)

original_interpretation: In November 2024 Intel said it planned to claim the investment tax credit, expected to be up to 25% of qualified investments, on more than US$100 billion of planned US investment.
evidence_found: "Intel also plans to claim the U.S. Treasury Department's Investment Tax Credit, which is expected to be up to 25% of qualified investments of more than $100 billion." (Intel 8-K Ex. 99.1, 26 Nov 2024)
notes: Superseded context: 48D rate became 35% for property placed in service after 2025; claim is correctly framed as a Nov 2024 statement.

original_interpretation: Under the August 2025 agreement Intel issued 274,583,000 shares to Commerce at closing in exchange for US$5.695 billion of accelerated CHIPS direct-funding disbursements (US$20.74 per share), and 158,740,000 shares into escrow at US$20.00 per share to be released as US$3.1748 billion of Secure Enclave disbursements are paid.
evidence_found: "274,583,000 Shares are to be issued to the DOC on the Closing Date ... corresponding to a $20.74 per share price"; "158,740,000 Shares are to be issued into escrow ... corresponding to a $20.00 per share price"; "$5,695,000,000" and "$3,174,800,000" (Intel 8-K, event date 22 Aug 2025, Item 1.01, re-opened 2026-09-30)

original_interpretation: The US$20.47 per-share price in Intel's announcement of the government stake is a blended figure: 433.3 million shares for US$8.87 billion combines US$20.74 per share for the accelerated CHIPS funds and US$20.00 per share for the Secure Enclave escrow shares.
evidence_found: Recomputed: 274,583,000 x 20.74 = 5,694.85m; 158,740,000 x 20.00 = 3,174.80m; total 8,869.65m / 433,323,000 shares = US$20.469 per share. Inputs confirmed in Intel 8-K (SRC-0315).
notes: Arithmetic is correct; inference classification is honest.

original_interpretation: Commerce received a five-year warrant to buy up to 240,516,150 Intel shares at US$20.00, exercisable only if Intel ceases to own directly or indirectly at least 51% of its foundry business.
evidence_found: Warrants for "240,516,150 shares of common stock" at "$20.00 per share", exercisable only "if...the Company ceases to directly or indirectly own at least 51% of its foundry business", and "will expire on the fifth anniversary of the Closing Date." (Intel 8-K, 25 Aug 2025)

original_interpretation: Intel's obligations under its CHIPS Direct Funding Agreement are considered discharged (other than for the Secure Enclave), and the government has no further obligations under that agreement once the released funds are paid.
evidence_found: "the Company's obligations pursuant to the DFA will be considered discharged (other than with respect to Secure Enclave), and ... the US Government will have no further obligations under the DFA" (Intel 8-K, 25 Aug 2025)

original_interpretation: Commerce agreed to vote its Intel shares in line with the Intel board's nominees and recommendations, with limited exceptions.
evidence_found: DOC "must vote any shares of common stock held by it in favor of the nominees of and any proposals recommended by the Company's Board", with exceptions (paraphrase) for matters violating the agreement or materially affecting government interests/compliance (Intel 8-K, 25 Aug 2025)

original_interpretation: On 27 August 2025 Intel received the full US$5.695 billion accelerated CHIPS disbursement and issued Commerce 274,583,000 shares, a warrant for up to 240,516,150 shares and 158,740,000 escrowed shares.
evidence_found: "On August 27, 2025 (the 'Closing Date'), the closing occurred under the Purchase Agreement" ... "the Company received the full amount of the accelerated disbursements under the DFA of $5.695 billion"; issued "274,583,000 shares of common stock", "a warrant to purchase up to 240,516,150 shares", and "158,740,000 shares" into escrow (Intel 8-K, filed 29 Aug 2025)
notes: Filing date is 29 Aug 2025; source publication_date '2025-08' is consistent.

original_interpretation: Treasury and the IRS issued final regulations for the section 48D credit as T.D. 10009, published 23 October 2024 and effective 23 December 2024.
evidence_found: "T.D. 10009"; Federal Register Vol. 89, No. 205, 23 October 2024; "DATES: Effective date: These regulations are effective on December 23, 2024." (T.D. 10009, 89 FR, 23 Oct 2024, re-opened 2026-09-30)

original_interpretation: Under the 48D final regulations, if a taxpayer undertakes a significant transaction materially expanding semiconductor capacity in a foreign country of concern within 10 years of placing property in service, it must repay 100 percent of the 48D credits previously allowed.
evidence_found: "if there is an applicable transaction by an applicable taxpayer before the close of the 10-year period beginning on the date such taxpayer placed in service property that is eligible for the section 48D credit, then the taxpayer's Federal income tax liability ... must be increased by 100 percent of the aggregate decrease in the credits allowed" ; "applicable transaction means ... any significant transaction involving the material expansion of semiconductor manufacturing capacity of such applicable taxpayer in any foreign country of concern." (T.D. 10009, 89 FR, 23 Oct 2024, re-opened 2026-09-30)
notes: An exception applies if the transaction is ceased or abandoned within 45 days of IRS notice (sec. 50(a)(3)(B)).

original_interpretation: Under the 48D final regulations, construction can be shown to have begun either by the physical work test or by a 5 percent safe harbor (paying or incurring 5% of the facility's expected basis), subject to a continuity requirement.
evidence_found: "(d) Five percent safe harbor--(1) In general. Construction of a property will be considered as having begun if: (i) A taxpayer pays or incurs ... five percent or more of the total cost of the property; and (ii) Thereafter, the taxpayer maintains continuous construction or continuous efforts." and "(c) Physical work test--(1) In general. Under the physical work test, construction of an item of property begins when physical work of a significant nature begins" (T.D. 10009, 89 FR, 23 Oct 2024, re-opened 2026-09-30, Sec. 1.48D-5(c)-(d))
correction: The safe harbor threshold is paying or incurring 5% or more of the total cost of the property (all costs properly included in the property's basis), measured per item of property or single advanced manufacturing facility project, not '5% of the facility's expected basis'. Superseding claim recorded.

original_interpretation: The IRS states the 48D credit is 25% of qualified investment for property placed in service through 31 December 2025 and 35% for qualified property placed in service thereafter.
evidence_found: "25% of the qualified investment for the taxable year" for property placed in service through December 31, 2025, and "35%" for qualified property placed in service thereafter (IRS Advanced manufacturing investment credit page, last reviewed or updated 27 Jul 2026, re-opened 2026-09-30)

original_interpretation: To receive the 48D credit as an elective (direct) payment a taxpayer must obtain a registration number through the IRS IRA/CHIPS pre-filing registration tool and file Forms 3468 and 3800 with its return.
evidence_found: Elective payment requires "a registration number using the IRA/CHIPS Pre-filing Registration Tool" and filing "the annual tax return by the due date (or extended due date)" with properly completed Forms 3468 and 3800 (IRS 48D page, updated 27 Jul 2026)

original_interpretation: Qualified 48D property must be tangible depreciable property integral to the operation of the advanced manufacturing facility placed in service after 31 December 2022, and excludes buildings or portions used for offices or administrative functions.
evidence_found: Qualified property must be "placed in service after Dec. 31, 2022", "tangible property that is subject to depreciation or amortization", "integral to the operation of an advanced manufacturing facility"; excluded are buildings used for "offices, administrative services, or other functions unrelated to manufacturing" (IRS 48D page)

original_interpretation: OMB's Federal Program Inventory describes the 48D credit as 25% and states that construction on qualifying facilities must commence by 31 December 2025.
evidence_found: "The credit is 25 percent for qualified property placed into service after December 31, 2022." and "Construction on a qualified facility must begin by December 31, 2025." (OMB Federal Program Inventory, TC.087, re-opened 2026-09-30)
notes: The claim accurately reports what OMB says, but OMB's content is wrong/stale: 48D(e) excludes only property whose construction begins after 31 Dec 2026 (T.D. 10009 preamble, SRC-0318), and the rate is 35% for property placed in service after 2025 (IRS, SRC-0319). Do not use this claim as evidence of the deadline; existing contradiction CON-0029 covers it.

original_interpretation: At enactment, CBO/JCT scored the CHIPS Act's 25% advanced manufacturing investment credit at US$24.3 billion of lost revenue over 2022-2031 (US$22.1 billion through 2026).
evidence_found: Table row: "Advanced Manufacturing Investment Tax Credit | $22.1 billion | $24.3 billion" (columns 2022-2026 and 2022-2031); "CBO estimates the tax credit would decrease tax revenue by $22.1 billion through 2026." (CRFB, 22 Jul 2022, citing CBO cost estimate for H.R. 4346, publication 58319)
notes: Secondary summary of a CBO/JCT score; the CBO document itself was not opened. Outdated as a current cost estimate given the 2025 rate increase to 35%, but the claim is explicitly framed 'at enactment'.
